name: Pretraining
summary: Training a model from scratch on huge amounts of text by asking it, over and over, to predict the next token and correcting its mistakes.

D1.guide: Try it: cover the next word in a sentence and guess it.
text: Imagine reading millions of books where the next word is always covered. You guess, peek, and learn a tiny bit from every wrong guess.
Do that trillions of times and you become very good at guessing. That's pretraining.
D1.analogy: Guess the covered word, then peek.

text: The training objective is simple: for each position in a batch of text, predict the next token. The difference between the prediction and the real token is the **loss**.
**Gradient descent** nudges every weight slightly to reduce that loss, batch after batch, on large GPU clusters.
Loss tends to fall predictably as models, data and compute grow together (**scaling laws**). The result is a **base model** that continues text but doesn't yet follow instructions.
D2.analogy: Guess the covered word, then peek.
D2.analogyBreaks: A reader understands the story while guessing. The model only adjusts numbers to make the right token more likely; abilities like arithmetic or translation emerge unevenly from that single objective.

predict.question: You type a question into a freshly pretrained base model. What does it usually do?
options: Continues the text, perhaps with more questions or an unrelated paragraph
predict.explanation: A base model has only learned to continue text; following instructions comes from post-training.

text: Pretraining is one loop repeated many times: **predict** the next piece of text, **compare** with what really came next, and **nudge** the model's numbers so the right answer gets a little more likely.
Here is that loop at toy size. The model has one score for every pair of characters, so it can only look one character back. Press **Train** and watch the loss fall and the guesses sharpen.

interactiveConfig.note: Same idea as real pretraining, at a scale of about 700 numbers instead of billions.
interactiveConfig.text: the quiet queen sat by the window and watched the rain. she asked a question that no one in the hall could answer. the quick brown fox ran across the field, then the hen and the cat ran after it. there is a thin thread of thought that runs through the whole of this short text: what comes next depends on what came before. after a t you often see an h, and after a q you almost always see a u. a model that learns these habits has learned something true about the text, even if it knows nothing else at all. it cannot spell whole words, but it can guess the next letter better than chance. that is the start of learning to write.

tasks: Choose q, then press Train a few times. How sure does the model become about u?
Choose e. Why does its top guess never get close to 100%?
Press Write 60 characters before training, then again after 10 clicks of Train. What changed?

predict.question: If you keep pressing Train, how low can the loss go?
options: Down to a floor above zero, then it stops
It falls, then climbs back up
predict.explanation: Looking one character back, the model cannot know whether “e” is followed by a space, an r or an n. The best it can do is match how often each follows. That floor is the dashed “best possible” line.

text: The model is a table of scores *W[a][b]*. Softmax turns row *a* into probabilities *p(b|a)* for the character after *a*. The **loss** is the average of −log *p* of the character that really came next, over every pair in the text.

The gradient for each score is simple: (*n_a* × *p(b|a)* − count(*a*→*b*)) ÷ *N*, where *n_a* is how often *a* appears and *N* is the number of pairs. Gradient descent subtracts the **learning rate** η times that gradient from every score, every step.
Change η and watch the curve. Too small and it crawls. Too large and each step overshoots, so the loss bounces or climbs.

interactiveConfig.note: The learning rates look large because the loss is averaged over every pair in the text, which makes each gradient small.
interactiveConfig.text: the quiet queen sat by the window and watched the rain. she asked a question that no one in the hall could answer. the quick brown fox ran across the field, then the hen and the cat ran after it. there is a thin thread of thought that runs through the whole of this short text: what comes next depends on what came before. after a t you often see an h, and after a q you almost always see a u. a model that learns these habits has learned something true about the text, even if it knows nothing else at all. it cannot spell whole words, but it can guess the next letter better than chance. that is the start of learning to write.

tasks: Set η to about 2 and press Step ×100. Then Reset, set η back to 20 and do the same. Compare the loss.
Set η to about 500 and step. What does the curve do, and does the “best possible” line get any closer?
Choose e and train until the loss stops falling. Compare the Share and p columns. What has the model learned?
D4.code:
W = small_random(V, V)              # W[a][b]: score for b following a
repeat steps times:
    loss, grad = 0, zeros(V, V)
    for a, b in pairs(text):        # every character and the one after it
        p = softmax(W[a])           # predict
        loss -= log(p[b])           # compare
        grad[a] += p                # push every guess down a little...
        grad[a][b] -= 1             # ...and the right answer up
    W -= lr * grad / N              # nudge (N = number of pairs)
tradeoffs: A higher learning rate learns faster until it overshoots; real training warms the rate up and then lowers it over time.
This toy uses the whole text every step. Real pretraining uses random batches: each step is far cheaper, but noisier.
Looking one character back caps how good the model can get. Longer context and bigger models lower that floor, at the cost of much more compute.
Lower training loss is not the goal on its own: a model that memorises its training text can do worse on new text.

predict.question: You raise the learning rate from 20 to 500 and train. What happens to the loss?
options: It jumps around and ends up higher than where it started
predict.explanation: Each step moves the scores so far that it overshoots the minimum, so the loss bounces and climbs above the starting value instead of settling.

text: Open questions: how much more high-quality data exists, the balance between model size and training tokens (compute-optimal scaling), whether some abilities emerge suddenly or only look sudden, and how much synthetic data can substitute for human text.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
